item.title: New Xbox Console Update for September 2026 Quietly Released
item.description:
Xbox has quietly rolled out a new console update for September 2026, bringing several fixes to the Xbox Series X, Series S, and Xbox One. While the update is focused primarily on maintenance rather than major user-facing features, there are separate signs that more substantial Xbox system changes are currently in development.

The modest public release comes as Microsoft continues testing much more noticeable console changes through its never-ending Xbox Insider program. Recent examples include the Xbox Disc to Digital scheme, which entered Insider testing in August 2026, alongside selectable startup animations, additional profile customization options, improved console search, and higher-quality Remote Play. On September 9, Microsoft announced that members of the Alpha and Alpha Skip-Ahead Insiders tiers could begin testing Remote Play at up to 1440p as part of another batch of experimental features.

First Next-Gen PS6, Xbox Helix Console Specs Leak Online

New alleged PS6 and Xbox Helix specifications offer an early glimpse at next generation console performance and potential differences.

1
By Adrian Morales

September 2026 Xbox Console Update Introduces 4 Fixes

According to Microsoft's official changelog, the latest version of its console OS began rolling out on September 22, fixing an issue that prevented the Share button from being remapped through the Xbox Accessories app. It also addresses errors triggered by certain search terms and crashes that could occur when opening the Manage queue page in the "My games and apps" menu. Microsoft additionally lists unspecified stability and performance improvements, making this a considerably smaller public-facing release than many Xbox updates that debuted earlier in 2026.

  • Various stability and performance fixes.

item.title: 7 Single-Player FPS Games Perfect From Beginning To End
item.description:
First-person shooter games might prioritize multiplayer these days, but nothing can beat a tight single-player campaign. Even mediocre ones are a lot of fun, while the best examples keep the action rolling for a perfect few hours. These FPS games resist the urge to add unnecessary padding through massive open-world maps or side quests, instead maintaining peak momentum while respecting our time.

If you are exhausted by 30-hour marathons with occasional moments of brilliance, these shooters should be the ideal pick-me-up, as they hit the bullseye from their opening level to the credits (and maybe even beyond for repeat playthroughs). Fleeting perfection is hard to achieve, and these FPS games somehow keep it going for their entire campaigns.

Titanfall 2 Is The Gold Standard For Campaign Momentum

A Single-Player FPS Romp That Never Lets Up

  • Runtime: 6 Hours

OK, let's get the most obvious one out of the way. Along with great multiplayer, Titanfall 2 features the strongest single-player FPS campaign of the 2010s , which still means something, even as the genre gradually declined over the decade. Nowadays, we are used to Call of Duty tacking on a 5-player campaign to shut up players, but TF2 doesn't treat its single-player as a distraction that exists solely to meet a directive.

Over its 6 hours, the game constantly shakes things up, introducing new gimmicks while changing the environment. The time-jumping "Effect and Cause" level feels completely different than the platformer-driven "Into the Abyss," and that extends to the other 7 missions. The distinct chapters stand well on their own while still combining to create a whole greater than the sum of its parts.

Titanfall 2 smashes together two opposing playstyles that, somehow, complement each other flawlessly. Jack Cooper is basically a parkour tech ninja who moves blisteringly fast but also goes down easily; conversely, Jack's partner, BT-7274, is a towering mech who moves deliberately and hits like a tank. The campaign constantly swaps between the two, ensuring neither overstays its welcome.

10 First-Person Action Games That Are Incredible From Start To Finish

It's hard to find quality that endures from beginning to end, but that's exactly what you'll get in these action-packed first-person games.

1
By Ollie Tuscarny

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon Is Anti-Ubisoft Perfection

A Relentless Explosion That Just Keeps Getting Bigger And Louder

  • Runtime: 5 Hours

I generally enjoy Ubisoft's Far Cry games, but their repetitive open-world design makes achieving uniform perfection nearly impossible. In many ways, Blood Dragon strips away the bloat to craft a masterclass that highlights Far Cry 3 's top-notch gunplay without all the friction that tends to come with it. A standalone expansion that satirizes its franchise and pays homage to '80s action movies, Blood Dragon begins by mocking condescending tutorials, then immediately rips into glorious, over-the-top mayhem with a cool aesthetic.

Unlike the mainline entries, Blood Dragon casts you as a super soldier who can wreck armies single-handedly , letting you enjoy the power fantasy element instantly while still providing a sense of escalation through its instruments of battle (aka, guns). However, due to being entirely designed around countering a cyber commando, the campaign actually offers a consistent challenge, way more than the core open-world games.

Turbo Overkill Is All Rev, All The Time

Movement Shooter Excellence With Boomer Shooter Vibes

  • Runtime: 12 Hours

Quite a few boomer shooters fit this article, and I considered going with Ultrakill , Dusk , or even Cultic ; however, Turbo Overkill has a chainsaw leg, so any other argument is invalid. As awesome as this FPS subgenre has proven to be, its games occasionally stick too closely to the classics' blueprints, paying homage without bringing anything new to the table. Turbo Overkill avoids this pitfall by mainly playing like a movement shooter .

You can tell that an action game will be awesome if its main movement mechanic happens to also be its deadliest weapon. Turbo Overkill swaps your leg for a motorized chainsaw, instantly transforming every slide into a bloody meat blender that also lets you pull off absurd feats of agility and recharge your shield. Environments come back with half-pipes, curves, and catwalks, encouraging players to keep their feet off the ground like a superpowered skateboarder.

At more than 10 hours, Turbo Overkill is longer than most linear FPS games, but it maintains momentum by splitting its campaign into three episodes AND giving each weapon an outrageous alternate-fire mode that offers style and tactics.

Wolfenstein: The Old Blood Cuts The Filler To Become All Stellar

Who Doesn't Love Some Gothic Horror In Their Military FPS Game?

  • Runtime: 6 Hours

Kudos to Machine Games; all its first three Wolfenstein games made the shortlist for this article. The New Order and The New Colossus arguably reach more impressive highs (while being twice as long), but The Old Blood is the definition of "all killer, no filler." You don't waste time rummaging through Kreisau Circle or Eva's Hammer in search of collectibles that add virtually nothing to the experience; in comparison, The Old Blood never stops moving forward.

As a love letter to Return to Castle Wolfenstein , this standalone prequel steadily sprints through 2 parts, each with 4 chapters. Revolving around an infiltration, the first half plays out like The New Order , albeit with a heavier focus on stealth. Meanwhile, part 2 moves the action to Wulfburg and shifts the genre towards gothic and occult horror, producing the best 3-hour spell in modern Wolfenstein .

8 Near-Perfect FPS Games That Are Certified Flops

A first-person shooter can do everything right and still fail to meet commercial expectations. This FPS games didn't find a big enough audience.

4
By Ollie Tuscarny

Condemned: Criminal Origins Is Terrifyingly Perfect

A Survival Horror First-Person Action Shooter Masterpiece

  • Runtime: 7 Hours

I almost never complete a game in a single sitting. Condemned: Criminal Origins is one of the few exceptions, as it captured my attention in a unique way compared to most other releases. Prioritizing melee combat while presenting guns as a "dire straits" option, this classic is admittedly more survival horror than FPS, but it has enough elements of the latter to qualify as a recommendation. First-person melee rarely feels great, but Condemned pulls it off by presenting brutality as a demonstration of the protagonist's desperation .

Rather than slashing smoothly like in Red Steel 2 or Shadow Warrior , you swing a pipe wildly in the hope of bludgeoning an enraged enemy before they do the same to you. When things get extra hairy, your non-lethal stun gun becomes your most important tool for survival, buying you just enough time to land a clean blow or shot. From a haunting secondary school to a mannequin-filled department store, Condemned cycles through new environments, each with its own atmospheric flavor.

What can I say, Criminal Origins is just an unusually airtight FPS game .

F.E.A.R. Was And Will Always Be Perfect

GOAP, Destruction, And Dread

  • Runtime: 8 Hours

I probably talk about F.E.A.R. too often, but it's one of the greatest FPS games of all time. It has also aged well, something that cannot be said for every decades-old shooter with innovative tech. Along with well-done horror elements, Monolith set its 2005 project apart with GOAP AI, which lets enemies react appropriately (and announce their counter plans) to a developing problem rather than follow scripted sequences or charge blindly.

This system still feels ahead of the curve in many ways, and it rewards players who replay the campaign while utilizing different strategies. Beyond GOAP, F.E.A.R. just nails everything you expect from a top-class FPS game.

  • The guns are unique and feel good, and they can absolutely obliterate environments.
  • The slow-motion bullet time pays homage to Hong Kong cinema while serving as a genuine tool, not just a visual spectacle.
  • The campaign knows when to quiet the noise and pause the explosions, letting you exist in silence for a time.
  • New enemies are introduced at a good rate, culminating in a fantastic third act set in the Origin facility.
  • Alma Wade is creepy.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger Is One Heck Of A Western Ride

Arcade Shooting Goodness

  • Runtime: 5 Hours

Western shooters are in short supply in general, let alone ones that approach perfection. Aside from Red Dead Redemption and maybe Wild Arms , Call of Juarez is the best-known western video game series, and nearly all its entries are great (except The Cartel ​​​​​​, the only one not set in the Wild West) . If Gunslinger proves to be the franchise's final shot, Call of Juarez would have walked into the sunset at its absolute peak.

Told via an unreliable narrator who changes his story in the middle of gameplay, Gunslinger doesn't take itself remotely seriously, and that's a good thing. As a pastiche of Spaghetti Westerns, the game doesn't sacrifice fun for realism, and the gunplay has an arcade flow that feels and looks great. You have a combo multiplier, bullet time, a last-second dodge for extra coolness, and cinematic duels.

First-person shooter games might prioritize multiplayer these days, but nothing can beat a tight single-player campaign. Even mediocre ones are a lot of fun, while the best examples keep the action rolling for a perfect few hours. These FPS games resist the urge to add unnecessary padding through massive open-world maps or side quests, instead maintaining peak momentum while respecting our time.

If you are exhausted by 30-hour marathons with occasional moments of brilliance, these shooters should be the ideal pick-me-up, as they hit the bullseye from their opening level to the credits (and maybe even beyond for repeat playthroughs). Fleeting perfection is hard to achieve, and these FPS games somehow keep it going for their entire campaigns.

Titanfall 2 Is The Gold Standard For Campaign Momentum

A Single-Player FPS Romp That Never Lets Up

  • Runtime: 6 Hours

OK, let's get the most obvious one out of the way. Along with great multiplayer, Titanfall 2 features the strongest single-player FPS campaign of the 2010s , which still means something, even as the genre gradually declined over the decade. Nowadays, we are used to Call of Duty tacking on a 5-player campaign to shut up players, but TF2 doesn't treat its single-player as a distraction that exists solely to meet a directive.

Over its 6 hours, the game constantly shakes things up, introducing new gimmicks while changing the environment. The time-jumping "Effect and Cause" level feels completely different than the platformer-driven "Into the Abyss," and that extends to the other 7 missions. The distinct chapters stand well on their own while still combining to create a whole greater than the sum of its parts.

Titanfall 2 smashes together two opposing playstyles that, somehow, complement each other flawlessly. Jack Cooper is basically a parkour tech ninja who moves blisteringly fast but also goes down easily; conversely, Jack's partner, BT-7274, is a towering mech who moves deliberately and hits like a tank. The campaign constantly swaps between the two, ensuring neither overstays its welcome.

10 First-Person Action Games That Are Incredible From Start To Finish

It's hard to find quality that endures from beginning to end, but that's exactly what you'll get in these action-packed first-person games.

1
By Ollie Tuscarny

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon Is Anti-Ubisoft Perfection

A Relentless Explosion That Just Keeps Getting Bigger And Louder

  • Runtime: 5 Hours

I generally enjoy Ubisoft's Far Cry games, but their repetitive open-world design makes achieving uniform perfection nearly impossible. In many ways, Blood Dragon strips away the bloat to craft a masterclass that highlights Far Cry 3 's top-notch gunplay without all the friction that tends to come with it. A standalone expansion that satirizes its franchise and pays homage to '80s action movies, Blood Dragon begins by mocking condescending tutorials, then immediately rips into glorious, over-the-top mayhem with a cool aesthetic.

Unlike the mainline entries, Blood Dragon casts you as a super soldier who can wreck armies single-handedly , letting you enjoy the power fantasy element instantly while still providing a sense of escalation through its instruments of battle (aka, guns). However, due to being entirely designed around countering a cyber commando, the campaign actually offers a consistent challenge, way more than the core open-world games.

Turbo Overkill Is All Rev, All The Time

Movement Shooter Excellence With Boomer Shooter Vibes

  • Runtime: 12 Hours

Quite a few boomer shooters fit this article, and I considered going with Ultrakill , Dusk , or even Cultic ; however, Turbo Overkill has a chainsaw leg, so any other argument is invalid. As awesome as this FPS subgenre has proven to be, its games occasionally stick too closely to the classics' blueprints, paying homage without bringing anything new to the table. Turbo Overkill avoids this pitfall by mainly playing like a movement shooter .

You can tell that an action game will be awesome if its main movement mechanic happens to also be its deadliest weapon. Turbo Overkill swaps your leg for a motorized chainsaw, instantly transforming every slide into a bloody meat blender that also lets you pull off absurd feats of agility and recharge your shield. Environments come back with half-pipes, curves, and catwalks, encouraging players to keep their feet off the ground like a superpowered skateboarder.

At more than 10 hours, Turbo Overkill is longer than most linear FPS games, but it maintains momentum by splitting its campaign into three episodes AND giving each weapon an outrageous alternate-fire mode that offers style and tactics.

Find the odd one out before the timer hits zero.

Which one doesn't belong?

—

More Games

Wolfenstein: The Old Blood Cuts The Filler To Become All Stellar

Who Doesn't Love Some Gothic Horror In Their Military FPS Game?

  • Runtime: 6 Hours

Kudos to Machine Games; all its first three Wolfenstein games made the shortlist for this article. The New Order and The New Colossus arguably reach more impressive highs (while being twice as long), but The Old Blood is the definition of "all killer, no filler." You don't waste time rummaging through Kreisau Circle or Eva's Hammer in search of collectibles that add virtually nothing to the experience; in comparison, The Old Blood never stops moving forward.

As a love letter to Return to Castle Wolfenstein , this standalone prequel steadily sprints through 2 parts, each with 4 chapters. Revolving around an infiltration, the first half plays out like The New Order , albeit with a heavier focus on stealth. Meanwhile, part 2 moves the action to Wulfburg and shifts the genre towards gothic and occult horror, producing the best 3-hour spell in modern Wolfenstein .

8 Near-Perfect FPS Games That Are Certified Flops

A first-person shooter can do everything right and still fail to meet commercial expectations. This FPS games didn't find a big enough audience.

4
By Ollie Tuscarny

Condemned: Criminal Origins Is Terrifyingly Perfect

A Survival Horror First-Person Action Shooter Masterpiece

  • Runtime: 7 Hours

I almost never complete a game in a single sitting. Condemned: Criminal Origins is one of the few exceptions, as it captured my attention in a unique way compared to most other releases. Prioritizing melee combat while presenting guns as a "dire straits" option, this classic is admittedly more survival horror than FPS, but it has enough elements of the latter to qualify as a recommendation. First-person melee rarely feels great, but Condemned pulls it off by presenting brutality as a demonstration of the protagonist's desperation .

Rather than slashing smoothly like in Red Steel 2 or Shadow Warrior , you swing a pipe wildly in the hope of bludgeoning an enraged enemy before they do the same to you. When things get extra hairy, your non-lethal stun gun becomes your most important tool for survival, buying you just enough time to land a clean blow or shot. From a haunting secondary school to a mannequin-filled department store, Condemned cycles through new environments, each with its own atmospheric flavor.

What can I say, Criminal Origins is just an unusually airtight FPS game .

F.E.A.R. Was And Will Always Be Perfect

GOAP, Destruction, And Dread

  • Runtime: 8 Hours

I probably talk about F.E.A.R. too often, but it's one of the greatest FPS games of all time. It has also aged well, something that cannot be said for every decades-old shooter with innovative tech. Along with well-done horror elements, Monolith set its 2005 project apart with GOAP AI, which lets enemies react appropriately (and announce their counter plans) to a developing problem rather than follow scripted sequences or charge blindly.

This system still feels ahead of the curve in many ways, and it rewards players who replay the campaign while utilizing different strategies. Beyond GOAP, F.E.A.R. just nails everything you expect from a top-class FPS game.

  • The guns are unique and feel good, and they can absolutely obliterate environments.
  • The slow-motion bullet time pays homage to Hong Kong cinema while serving as a genuine tool, not just a visual spectacle.
  • The campaign knows when to quiet the noise and pause the explosions, letting you exist in silence for a time.
  • New enemies are introduced at a good rate, culminating in a fantastic third act set in the Origin facility.
  • Alma Wade is creepy.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger Is One Heck Of A Western Ride

Arcade Shooting Goodness

  • Runtime: 5 Hours

Western shooters are in short supply in general, let alone ones that approach perfection. Aside from Red Dead Redemption and maybe Wild Arms , Call of Juarez is the best-known western video game series, and nearly all its entries are great (except The Cartel ​​​​​​, the only one not set in the Wild West) . If Gunslinger proves to be the franchise's final shot, Call of Juarez would have walked into the sunset at its absolute peak.

Told via an unreliable narrator who changes his story in the middle of gameplay, Gunslinger doesn't take itself remotely seriously, and that's a good thing. As a pastiche of Spaghetti Westerns, the game doesn't sacrifice fun for realism, and the gunplay has an arcade flow that feels and looks great. You have a combo multiplier, bullet time, a last-second dodge for extra coolness, and cinematic duels.

item.title: Graveyard Keeper 2: Fishing Guide
item.description:
No crafting survival experience would be complete without a cozy fishing minigame, and that is no different in Graveyard Keeper 2 . Players can fish at multiple locations, including a spot just to the west of their house. You'll of course need a rod, and for more advanced fish, bait is required too. The difficult part is knowing when to pull or not. Essentially, when the yellow exclamation mark appears, you should hold and pull . When it disappears, or the line turns red, let go.

How to Increase Maximum Town Gratitude in Graveyard Keeper 2

Learn how to increase your maximum Town Gratitude in Graveyard Keeper 2, as well as the best ways to earn Gratitude.

By Joe Grantham

How To Fish In Graveyard Keeper 2

item.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake's New Map Just Drew a Line Final Fantasy 7 Remake Was Willing to Cross
item.description:
Nintendo has finally revealed the official map for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2, and surprisingly (or perhaps unsurprisingly after its big reveal), there aren't too many differences between it and the map of the original game. One of the debates I have been continually revisiting since the curtains were pulled back on Ocarina of Time 's gameplay during The Legend of Zelda 's 40th Anniversary Direct is whether a full-blown remake should evolve and completely transform the original game or simply polish it to make it look and feel more modern. Over the years, we have seen plenty of different examples of remakes that come from both sides of the aisle, but two of the more recent examples are The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Square Enix's Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy.

In fact, I would argue that there aren't two better recent examples out there, as, based on what we've been shown so far, the Ocarina of Time remake is one of the most faithful remakes I've ever seen, while the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy has become infamous for, in the eyes of some, taking things a bit too far. I have personally adored everything Square Enix has done with the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy up to this point, and I have a feeling I'm going to love the direction Nintendo took the original Ocarina of Time in the remake. However, the official reveal of Ocarina of Time 's new map of Hyrule has me once again considering whether faithfulness or evolution is the right way to go with a remake, and I stand on that line with my thoughts because choosing either side is a divisive choice, no matter your argument.

Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Is Facing the Hardest Part of Bringing Back a Classic

Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake is walking a difficult line between honoring a classic and proving its old design still works today.

12
By Josh Cotts

Ocarina of Time Remake's New Map Isn't All That New

Looking at the new Ocarina of Time map side by side with the one from the original game, the biggest thing that stands out to me is how quickly I can tell where everything is. Death Mountain is still looming over the northeastern corner of Hyrule, Zora's Domain is tucked away to the east, Lake Hylia is down south, and Gerudo Valley still stretches off toward the west. There are certainly differences if you start looking closely enough, and we've already seen that some individual locations are going to be much larger once we actually get inside them, but Nintendo hasn't used the remake as an excuse to redraw Hyrule simply because it now has the hardware to do so.

More Games

That's probably more important than it sounds, especially after everything else Nintendo has changed. The remake gives Link far more modern movement, including a manual jump and sprint, while the free camera alone changes how players will interact with spaces originally designed around the limitations of the Nintendo 64. Castle Town has been expanded, Kokiri Forest has more room to breathe, and even something as simple as the continuous day-night cycle means Hyrule is no longer going to operate exactly the way it did in 1998. Nintendo clearly isn't afraid to touch the original game, but the new map suggests it has also decided there are certain things it simply doesn't need to touch.

The new map still leaves one major question unanswered: whether Nintendo is being this conservative with Ocarina of Time ’s dungeons too, or whether those are where the remake will finally take bigger liberties.

I actually think that's where the remake has started becoming much more interesting to me, because faithfulness isn't necessarily the same thing as refusing to change anything. Nintendo seems more interested in asking how much of the original game it can preserve while removing the limitations it was once confined to. If Kokiri Forest can be bigger without becoming a different place, there isn't much reason not to make it bigger. If Castle Town can have more streets and buildings while still looking like the Castle Town players remember, expanding it doesn't really come at the expense of anything. The map suggests Nintendo is taking that same approach to Hyrule itself, where the goal isn't to replace what was there but to finally give it the space it may have always deserved.

Final Fantasy 7 Remake Was Willing to Change the Blueprint

Square Enix took a very different approach with Final Fantasy 7 Remake , and Midgar is probably the easiest place to see it. The original game's opening section in Midgar was turned into an entire game, which meant Square Enix couldn't simply rebuild the same areas at a larger scale and call it a day. Places that were once passed through relatively quickly suddenly needed enough depth to support dozens of hours, while characters and events that occupied a much smaller place in the original story were given significantly more room. By the time Final Fantasy 7 Remake reaches its ending, it becomes pretty clear that Square Enix isn't treating the original game's structure as something it has to preserve at all costs.

I actually think that's where the remake has started becoming much more interesting to me, because faithfulness isn't necessarily the same thing as refusing to change anything.

I loved that about Final Fantasy 7 Remake , and Rebirth only made me appreciate the decision more, but it also explains why the trilogy has remained so divisive. Once a remake starts changing more than the way an old game looks or plays, there is always going to be a point where someone feels like it crossed a line. For some players, expanding Midgar was probably already enough. For others, it was the changes to the story that followed. Square Enix was willing to risk that reaction because it decided there was more value in surprising people who already knew Final Fantasy 7 than there was in giving them exactly the game they remembered.

Ocarina of Time looks like it is heading in almost the opposite direction, and its new map may be the clearest example of that philosophy we've seen yet. Nintendo can make Hyrule bigger without moving Death Mountain somewhere else. It can turn Castle Town into a much more convincing place without replacing the town players already know. Even the remake's biggest changes so far seem designed to make exploring the same Hyrule easier or more natural rather than giving longtime players an entirely different version of it.

Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake's New Map Just Drew a Line Final Fantasy 7 Remake Was Willing to Cross

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Officially Confirms Paywalled Content
Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake and Fable Are Solving the Same Problem in Completely Different Ways

I'm still not convinced one approach is necessarily better than the other, either. Part of what made Final Fantasy 7 Remake so exciting for me was never knowing how far Square Enix was willing to go, while a huge part of what has me excited about Ocarina of Time is seeing places I've known for decades rebuilt without losing what made them recognizable in the first place. The more Nintendo shows of the remake, though, the clearer its answer to this whole debate seems to become. Ocarina of Time isn't being treated like something that needs to be reinvented. Nintendo seems to believe the game players remember is still good enough to be the blueprint, and the new map of Hyrule just drew that line more clearly than anything we've seen so far.
